newsitem.title: UK: Urals seen pressured by avails, Iraq news.
newsitem.headline: Urals seen pressured by avails, Iraq news.

text.p: Haitham Haddadin
Russian Urals was feeling the heat on Tuesday from unsold cargoes with buyers awaiting cheaper Iraqi sour, while West African grades were competing with North African oil, traders said.
In the Mediterranean, no definite deals were reported but the market was rife with rumours that Urals traded at a few cents stronger than last week.

Several trades however said the sour crude was in fact still weak, reeling from the pressure of unsold June avails. They said buyers and sellers were far apart at Dated Brent -$1.45 and -$1.35 respectively.
An Italian trader denied rumours that he sold a mid-June loader of the Russian sour crude to an independent trader at Dated Brent -$1.35, or five cents better than a deal last week.

"For sure there is an oversupply of Urals, and coupled with the margins that are not that good...we disagree with those saying that Urals is strengthening. We see the market weakening," an Italian refiner said.
There were four large and five small first and second decade June Urals cargoes still unsold, he said.
Buyers said they were on the sidelines taking their time before picking June Urals as they were awaiting Iraqi sour crude Kirkuk, a cheaper alternative, to start flowing again soon.
On Monday, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan recommended a renewal of Iraq's $2 billion "oil-for-food" deal for another six-months after the first period expires on June 7.
"The news is very reassuring, because Kofi Anan said we recommend a rollover of the deal. It remains to be seen when the first vessels (of Kirkuk) will be loaded," one trader said.

"There will probably not be a huge delay in terms of Kirkuk loadings...There will be a bit a Kirkuk and a bit of Urals available because right now there is very little Iranian on the market," the trader added.
Iraq, reeling under U.N. sanctions after its 1990 invasion of its small oil-rich neighbour Kuwait, uses the money from the oil sales to pay for food and medicine for its citizens.
West African traders said the market was continuing last week's slow pace with some grades steady but others weaker as several June cargoes are still looking for homes.
There was unconfirmed talk of a July 2-4 Pennington, a rarely traded grade, changing hands on Monday at a strong Dated Brent +95 cents.
Some traders said Algeria's state oil company Sonatrach was offering Saharan Blend to European traders at prices cheaper than Nigerian grades, making the latter less attractive to buyers.
"For Europe, North African is cheaper than the West African. Saharan Blend is being offered in the low fifties (premium to Dated Brent), I was offered some at that price," one trader said.

I think the West African grades are a little weaker in general...July barrels are being shown but in a very secretive sort of way, maybe because there's plenty of June cargoes (still unsold)," the trader said.
In particular, Qua Iboe was seen pressured, with one trader said to be holding an unsold VLCC of the Nigerian light grade.
Other traders, however, said most grades were assessed to be steady, like Bonny Light in the Dated Brent +50/55 cents region and Forcados at about a 25 cents premium to dated Brent.
"I think what is left in June will find homes in the U.S. Gulf," noted one trader, who said there were eight or nine June cargoes still unsold.
-- Haitham Haddadin, London newsroom +44 171 542 8145
